headline: Generative AI research is shifting from adoption to warrant, asking who may rely on a machine's output and on what terms, while the decolonial strand argues that the same platforms extract the knowledge they are asked to produce.
paras: The sharpest cluster this week is on warranted reliance. Qiang and Wang (2026) interviewed 25 university teachers and found them delegating cognitive work to GenAI while defending their judgement in the same breath. Umar (2026) turns that into a model: once GenAI is in the loop, visible performance stops being evidence of independent competence. Karnatak, Kleek and Shadbolt (2026, AIES) ask the prior normative question, when reliance is epistemically warranted rather than merely induced, and Berman and Smithies (2026, AIES) take the argument to the platform: they call the arrangement epistemic extractivism. For the professional criticality paper this is the week's spine, and it is now four sources deep instead of one.

On complexity the interesting item is Bakogianni, Liljekvist and Bui (2026), who use Engestrom's activity theory to treat GenAI as a runaway object that reconfigures roles and tools across teaching and research. Beside it sits a systematic review of how game-making curricula build systems thinking (Educational Research Review, 2026) and one deliberate wildcard: a Cognition paper (2026) that treats posture as a micro-ecological constraint on how a problem is posed. That last one is not education research, but it is the most literal empirical reading of enabling constraints that the radar has found, and it may earn a place in Substrate Matters as an aside.

The decolonial shelf is unusually strong. Zusman and Hollman (2026) show how journal hierarchies reproduce the power geometry of knowledge production and name pluriversal alternatives, which speaks directly to how the FUNGI corpus is assembled. Immonen (2026) finds pluriversal politics in anticolonial art workshops, and a Colombian case (White Rose, 2026) works with territorio as a vernacular security concept. On policy, the EU Critical Raw Materials Act reads as an extraction strategy under a just-transition label (EIST, 2026).

Two practical items close the week. A four-year participatory action research project in an Italian community-supported agriculture scheme concludes that research dependency became a crutch for the community it served (Action Research, 2026): read it before you promise participation again in the CDC course. And a Dutch pair in Tijdschrift voor Lerarenopleiders (Leuverink, Duijzer and Peltenburg, 2026) documents how onderzoekend vermogen was threaded through a whole pabo curriculum, which is the closest published template to Windesheim's own build.

About this run: it is a catch-up. The two previous weekly runs were degraded, so this one worked the window from 5 October, swept all 20 journals of the watch through Crossref by ISSN for the first time, and kept 28 of 209 candidates. Six lineage drafts are ready in the inbox and one lineage document is complete.
